title: Stack & Queue Design Problems
summary: Design questions that bolt an extra O(1) guarantee — minimum, capacity, bulk increment — onto a stack or queue, testing whether you can extend an interface without breaking its core cost promise.

slides.markdown:
"Design a stack or queue with an extra guarantee" is its own interview category, distinct from using a stack or queue as a tool inside a bigger algorithm. Min-stack, fixed-capacity circular queue, and an increment-supporting stack all ask the same underlying question: can you add one new O(1) operation to an existing structure **without** degrading any of its existing O(1) operations?

The answer, every time, is to carry a small amount of extra bookkeeping alongside the core structure — never to recompute the new guarantee by scanning, which would silently reintroduce an O(n) cost the design was supposed to avoid.

slides.subTitle: Tracking the running minimum without rescanning on every pop
slides.markdown:
A min-stack supports the usual push/pop/top plus `get_min()`, all in O(1). The naive idea — scan the whole stack on every `get_min()` call — is O(n) per call, which defeats the point.

The fix: maintain the minimum **incrementally**, updating it on every push and restoring the previous minimum on every pop, rather than recomputing it from scratch. That requires remembering not just the current minimum but the minimum *as it was before* the most recent push, since a pop needs to revert to that prior state — which is exactly what a second, parallel stack gives you for free.

slides.subTitle: Pushing (value, min-so-far) pairs
Memory vs simplicity
slides.markdown:
| | Pairs on main stack | Separate auxiliary min-stack |
|---|---|---|
| Memory per element | 2 values always | 1 value, plus a second stack entry only when the min changes (or a mirrored entry each push, depending on variant) |
| Code complexity | simplest — one structure | two structures kept in sync |
| Common mistake | none major | popping main stack without popping aux stack in lockstep |

An alternative design uses a separate auxiliary stack that only pushes a new minimum when a push actually lowers it (or, in a simpler but less memory-efficient variant, mirrors every push). Both approaches are O(1) on every operation; the pairs-on-one-stack version is usually easier to get right because there's only one structure to keep synchronized, at the cost of always storing two values per entry instead of one.

slides.sectionTitle: Designing a circular queue with fixed capacity
slides.markdown:
A fixed-capacity circular queue is the array-backed queue from the fundamentals topic, with explicit capacity enforcement added:

```python
class FixedCircularQueue:
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self._buf = [None] * capacity
        self._cap = capacity
        self._front = 0
        self._size = 0

    def enqueue(self, x):
        if self._size == self._cap:
            return False  # full
        self._buf[(self._front + self._size) % self._cap] = x
        self._size += 1
        return True

    def dequeue(self):
        if self._size == 0:
            return False  # empty
        self._front = (self._front + 1) % self._cap
        self._size -= 1
        return True
```

O(1) enqueue/dequeue, O(1) full/empty checks via the explicit `_size` counter rather than index comparison — which is precisely the detail the next slide's pitfall depends on.

slides.sectionTitle: Distinguishing a full queue from an empty one
slides.subTitle: When head equals tail
slides.markdown:
A circular queue implementation that tracks only `front` and `rear` indices (no separate size counter) hits a genuine ambiguity: both an **empty** queue and a **full** queue can have `front == rear`, since the rear index wraps around to meet the front exactly when the buffer fills up.

```python
# BUG: front == rear is treated as "empty" always,
# so a full queue is misreported as empty
def is_empty(self):
    return self._front == self._rear
```

Three common fixes: keep an explicit **size** counter (as in the previous slide — simplest, and what most production code does), always leave **one slot deliberately unused** so full and empty produce different index relationships, or keep a separate boolean flag that's set on the enqueue that causes the wrap and cleared on the next dequeue. Picking one of these upfront, rather than discovering the ambiguity while debugging, is the actual skill this pitfall tests.

slides.subTitle: Batching lazy updates instead of touching every element
slides.markdown:
A stack that supports "increment the bottom k elements by val" alongside normal push/pop looks like it needs O(k) work per increment call — touch every one of the bottom k elements and add val. Done naively, a sequence of many increment calls degrades badly.

The lazy-update trick: instead of applying the increment immediately, record it in a **separate array** at index `k - 1` (the deepest index the increment should still affect), meaning "whatever gets popped from position ≤ k-1 in the future should include this pending increment." On pop, apply any pending increment at the current top index to the value being returned, then **push that pending amount down** to the next index below (so it still applies to whatever's revealed next). This spreads the O(k) cost across up to k future pop calls instead of paying it all upfront.

slides.sectionTitle: Popping after a batched increment without adjusting the minimum
slides.markdown:
Combining the increment-stack idea with a min-stack is a natural follow-up question, and it exposes a subtle bug: a batched "increment the bottom k" operation changes stored values **without going through the normal push path**, so any minimum tracked per-entry (as in the min-stack pattern) can go stale unless it's explicitly recomputed for the affected range.

Concretely, if entry 3's stored `min_so_far` was computed assuming the original values below it, and a batch increment just raised several of those values, the cached minimum may now be **too low** — it reflects values that no longer exist in that form. Any design combining these two patterns needs to either recompute affected minimums explicitly after a batch update, or accept a relaxed guarantee (e.g., minimum is only exact between batch operations) and document that trade-off rather than silently returning a stale answer.

slides.sectionTitle: The shared skill across every design problem here
slides.markdown:
Min-stack, fixed-capacity circular queue, and the increment stack all reward the same discipline: identify the **one piece of extra state** that makes the new guarantee O(1), and update that state incrementally alongside every existing operation rather than recomputing it from the full structure on demand.

For min-stack, that state is the running minimum, carried per-entry. For the circular queue, it's an explicit size counter that disambiguates full from empty. For the increment stack, it's a lazily-propagated pending-increment value. None of these require a fundamentally new data structure — they require noticing exactly what small piece of memory, updated at the right moments, turns an O(n) recomputation into an O(1) lookup.
